# How the reviewers labelled commit messages

The labels in `gold/` come from Tian et al., *What Makes a Good Commit Message?* (ICSE 2022). The authors sampled
1,649 commit messages from five active Java projects (JUnit 4, OkHttp, Retrofit, Spring Boot, Dubbo) and labelled
each one with two questions:

- **What:** does the message summarise what was changed?
- **Why:** does it give the reason for the change?

**A good commit message has both.** Each message got one of four labels: why and what, no why, no what, neither.
Two authors labelled independently (Cohen's kappa 0.91) and a third settled disagreements. In a survey,
experienced open-source contributors labelled 120 of the messages; 102 of their labels (85%) matched the authors'.

The rest of this file is the authors' own coding of how messages express each part, from their released data
(`maintenance type and expression way.xlsx`, 252 messages coded).

## Ways a message says WHY (any one is enough)

| Category | Subcategories in their coding |
| --- | --- |
| Describe the issue | describes the error scenario; describes a shortcoming; introduces the issue report |
| Describe the objective | what the change is for, the goal it serves |
| Illustrate the requirement | something is out of date; the runtime or development environment changed; a usage need |
| Imply necessity | follows a convention or standard; improvements and benefits; relation to an implemented feature; relation to prior commits |
| Issue link or PR link | a reference to the issue or pull request the change belongs to counts as the reason |

Messages often have **no why** for: code refactoring, text file changes, typo fixes, annotation changes, version
management and test cases.

## Ways a message says WHAT

| Category | Subcategories in their coding |
| --- | --- |
| Summarise the code change | the object of change; a change list; characteristics of the change; contrast before and after |
| Illustrate the function | what the changed code now does |
| Describe the implementation principle | how the change works |

A message that only describes the problem (the why) without the change made has **no what**.

Source: dataset and coding at github.com/WhatMakesAGoodCM/What-Makes-a-Good-Commit-Message.

# Verdict rubric notes (short)

```yaml
criteria:
  - id: why                       # letters, digits, _ ; used in formulas as why_n (0..1)
    name: Says why
    inputs: [message]             # the gold set's input label
    scale: { type: binary, labels: [no, yes] }
    anchors: { no: "what a 'no' looks like", yes: "what a 'yes' looks like" }   # the judge picks between these
aggregation:
  method: formula                 # or weighted_mean
  formula: "what_n * why_n"       # comparisons and ?: work too
  normalize: [0, 100]
  passThreshold: 50               # passed = score >= 50; compared with the human pass/fail
```

- `context:` at the top is read by the judge for every criterion.
- Hand unsure messages to a human: on the judge, `minConfidence: 0.3, onLowConfidence: human`. Ratings whose
  confidence is below it wait for a person instead of counting. `check_against_humans` reports how many.
- `check_against_humans` also reports per-criterion agreement for criteria named `what` and `why`, the labels the
  gold set has.

content.text:
The rubric never reached 80% agreement with the humans. I used all 10 dev checks: it started at 57% and ended at 76%. On the held-out test set it scores the same 76% (66 of 87), with 9 messages handed to a human. `commit-review.yaml` is the only file I edited, and I never opened `gold/test.jsonl`.

**ROUNDS (gold/dev.jsonl)**

| Check | Agreement | Asked a human | What changed |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 55/96 = 57% | 0 | Baseline: the original style-rules criterion |
| 2 | 61/96 = 64% | 0 | Replaced the style criterion with "good = says what changed **and** why; style doesn't matter" |
| 3 | 75/96 = 78% | 0 | Codebook row: an issue or PR link counts as the why |
| 4 | 74/96 = 77% | 0 | Codebook row: a message that only describes the problem has no what |
| 5 | 75/96 = 78% | 0 | Setting: aggregation `weighted_mean` → `min` (no effect with one criterion; done so the next change could require both) |
| 6 | 73/96 = 76% | 0 | Added a separate `what` criterion (matched the humans' what label 71%) |
| 7 | 75/96 = 78% | 0 | Replaced `what`'s anchors with the codebook's "object of change" reading (what: 78%) |
| 8 | 72/96 = 75% | 0 | Replaced `good` with a `why` criterion built from the codebook's ways of saying why (why: 81%) |
| 9 | 68/91 = 75% | 5 | Setting: hand ratings below 0.1 confidence to a human |
| 10 | 61/81 = 75% | **15** | Setting: confidence cutoff raised to 0.2. Over the 12 cap, and no better |
| 11 | 68/89 = 76% | 7 | Setting: cutoff back to 0.1. Final rubric |

The last row is a re-check of the restored setting. It counts as the 10th change (the 11th call, since check 1 was the baseline) and is the run that confirmed the final rubric stays within the cap.

**Test result (gold/test.jsonl, one run):** 66 of 87 decided = **76%**, with 9 of 96 handed to a human (under the 12 cap). Per criterion: what 80%, why 83%.

The final rubric has two yes/no criteria, `what` and `why`. A message passes only if both are yes. Messages the judge is very unsure about (confidence below 0.1) go to a person.

**Why it stalled:**
- **Run-to-run noise.** The same rubric scored 77% and 78% on consecutive runs, so changes worth 1–2 points can't be told apart from chance.
- **Both criteria have to be right.** Each one matches the humans about 80–83% of the time, and a message only passes when both are right. That combination caps the overall figure in the mid-70s.
- **The labels are lenient on some kinds of message.** Humans marked bare messages like "Update README.md", "release 2.4.1" and "Added release notes" as having a why. The codebook says those kinds of change often have none, and the judge follows the codebook. Commits like "fix X bug (#123)" go the other way: humans usually say there's no what, and the judge disagrees.
- **Handing more to a human didn't help.** At 0.2 the judge handed over 15 messages and agreement stayed at 75%.

Getting past this would probably mean changing the design rather than making another one-line edit: for example, giving the judge worked examples written from the codebook (not taken from the gold set) for docs, release and dependency-bump commits. As it stands, it agrees with human reviewers about three times in four.
